speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I don't know if I told you about how they run away. Well, that was the thing that I had to, I guess I told you about how I had to walk. Yeah, yeah. Okay, well that's it. That's enough of that then. Well now wait though, about these ponies.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well. Now these ponies, were they wild ponies?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh they were Indian ponies. The Indians had a lot of them there. And there was one day, that was on the left of the old cabin, the one that dad first built when he homesteaded. And an old Indian buck come by there, and of course poor mother, dad was out harvesting. Mother was kind of scared of him, you know. Just little devils. They weren't only eight, nine years old. I was the oldest. And the only else he only had about, let's see, 97. Well if I was eight, or nine, Simon, the third boy would be, let's see, nine. He'd be two years old. He was just a baby. So, well he'd just, he moaned and he wanted something to eat, see. He couldn't talk English. Boy she fed him potatoes, cooked some potatoes. We did have potatoes that we'd raise during the summer. See we raised lots. That ground was raised good vegetables. That's all we had one, was a live off of them.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Potatoes and rutabagas and carrots. Us kids were full of vinegar, you know, we'd just run around. We didn't dare go outdoors. I told that before, I guess, about Will and had one pair of shoes a year. And the old man, when they bought them, you know, brought them home. All three of us started circling around with them. He made us come in, take them out. And that was in October when it was cold weather too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So your kids couldn't really go get around during the winter?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh no, we had to do our playing in the house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about chores? You still had to go out and do that?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No chores then. No, no chores then. No, Dad only had, well he had a cow and two Cayuses. That's all he had now. That's what I'm telling you, how he's struggling. That's all he had. That first winter, he didn't have feed. See to feed her, he had to feed his ponies. He had raised enough hay on that 12 acres that he had seeded. And he had butchered this cow, sowed half of it to buy this hay seed, the first year. And the next year, he had hay enough to sell to buy seed, flax seed, to sow. That's how he struggled. And I was the little boy then, had to walk them tracks four o 'clock in the morning. I guess I told you that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But now, these Indian ponies, could people pick them up if they wanted?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well they did, I tell you. You had to be careful. You had to get one that wasn't branded. If you get one that's branded, them Indians could make you trouble. There was an uncle of mine, Nado Swenson, for one. He picked one with an SP brand on it, brown, Nado. My uncle could ride a buck and horse to a tee, you know. He rode that thing over to Parkland. He got by with it because he went over there. Indians over here didn't catch him, see. And he traded that horse off. But that horse led him to bucking, but he rode him, he broke him to ride. And traded him off, see.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You said that your dad got into horses and that's where he made a little money. You said your dad got into horses and that's where he made a little money.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, he got into horse raising. That's what put him on his feet. After a few years, he just kept, he seen everybody. I tell you what, the Army come in there one time and bought horses. You know how much one farmer got for his horses? He got $600 for a nice gray Spanish… they were half-purchased… $600… they were well-matched, arch-necks. Oh, they were regular prize winners. They kept running the prices. The old man Rogers was the boy that sold them. And dad sold horses for around $250. $200 and $250 a horse. $400 and $500 a span. That's what put him on his feet. The grain didn't bring it. What little crop he had in grain, that didn't bring it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did he get his horses to start with? Where did he get his stock?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, there was a fellow named Setlow had a stallion. And he bred the mares to this stallion… see… and kept raising them. Saved all the mares he could. He'd have four, five, six colts a year. After he got lined out, see? That's how it come. And he wasn't the only one. Old Amos Frederiksen was another one. Raised horses. Well, when all the farmers started raising them. That could… see… but the great big farmers, they'd rather buy them than to raise them. A lot of them did. They just wasn't interested in raising them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, let me ask you a dumb question. Why was it that it was easier for him to make a little money raising horses than off of a little crop in his grass?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, that didn't bring nothing compared to horses. He just fed the stuff he raised. There's better, more money to feed it to these horses, don't you understand? Them days. Not only them. But he had that trouble of marketing with that, going that old grade with that one, that team. And did I tell you about how I wrecked when I was working for Dad?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You told me about the time you were going over the Clearwater River. That was a rough grade.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That old grade was a bad one. But it wasn't that that done it. I got over the grade.A lot of them didn't. West Thomas, he broke a leg there because his brake beam broke going down this 23 % grade. It was Steve part of it, 23 % in his locking. Right there's where my brake flew off. When I was a kid, 17, I had 440 sacks of wheat and four horses. And when that brake flew off, that wagon just shoved on my wheeler. And one of the wheelers went down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: One of the what?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: One of the wheelers fell down. See what I mean? And this brake, I told Dad, I wanted a long brake like the other farmers so he could reach it here, setting straight. You know, you had to stoop down like this to get a hold of it. A little bit of a catch bar like that that caused my foot to slip off when I hit this big rock. There was three of us guys, one farmer ahead of me, old Jimmy McBride and old Ryan Malcolm behind me. And Jimmy McBride's britching broke. He went fast. We were trying to beat a bunch of farmers we could see coming down the Melrose Ridge grade because if you didn't get down to the fair bowl first, ahead of them, you had to sit there and wait maybe two or three or four hours. You had to take your turn, don't you see? And so we all agreed that we had to hurry to get down there. Old Jimmy McBride was ahead and he stuck out and I stuck out. And of course I was close enough behind him I didn't see that big rock. I hit it.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That's what told my brake off because it knocked my foot off. And there I was, five feet of slack with my lines and I milked up the lines just as fast as I could. And I didn't want to get too close to the bank. I pulled a little bit but I didn't want to get too close. And I was just sat there like that, that old wagon, wide-tired wagon, shaking. And I finally decided I'd come put near going over. Just the only thing that put me back, I was clear out of the seat. The only thing that pulled me back was my lines. I had a good tight lines and I pulled back and I grabbed the seat like that, sat back in. I didn't try that brake no more. I just let her go. I went about 50 or 75 feet down that steep slope to where I got to where it was kind of a little bit more flat. And then, and this horse of dragon is what saved me. He had, he had fell with his back towards the tongue.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And the leaders, I had good leaders. Hadn't been for the good leaders, I wouldn't have made it. He had got his front feet in the lead bar and my leaders drug him down the hill. And the hind feet was just a swing and I was scared this was going to get under that wheel. See, I kept looking. If they had a wood, Jack knocked me off the grade. But it didn't because they kept pulling him. I had good leaders. Hadn't been for good leaders, as I say, I'd never made it. They just called him Gray Prince and another colt alongside him. This was, no, that was Ringbone Prince's good leader. This was Gray Prince I had that went down, just a colt. Oh, God. When I got down and got my brakes set, you know, that's when I come in to get scared. I was thinking fast, see. I got the brakes set and stopped. Old Malcolm behind me, he came down pretty close. I was pretty shaky. I was worried about it. I got him up, you know, and he stood there like this.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And I was afraid he broke his hip dragging him over them boulders. And Roy says, golly, how mercy. You come down there awful fast. Well, I said, I come down there like a bat out of hell, didn't I? I just joked. Roy, I said, when I get out, get this horse straightened around a little, I said, I'm going to pull out. Let you by. And I said, when you get to Peck, you tell that blacksmith, Sid Boyd, that I want this brake fixed just like yours so I can reach it and set it when I want it, without ease, not have to be stupid for it. And I said, I don't know what time I'll get home tonight. But I said, you tell Sid, I know Sid. He was a faithful, but you didn't dare bother Sid. He's a busy old black man, he had a pretty good temper. And now he was busy shooing horses, you know, a good horse shoer. I waited till he got to and he looked at you kind of mean, you know, like dark, complacent fellow.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I said, Sid, did Roy tell you what I wanted? Yes. He said, by God, he said, can't get it yet. It'll be after dinner.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: After dinner?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: After dinner… well, that's all right, Sid. I said, can you fix it today? Yeah. He said, OK, Sid. I'll just go put the horses up for dinner and feed them and get my dinner. I'll come back when you get ready. I said, by God, he did. But it's about midnight before I got home that night. And Dad wanted to know what's the matter. I said, you're lucky me and the horses come home alive, Dad. I said, by golly, I'll tell you. I got that break fixed. I don't care what the price is, but you got to pay old Sid Boyd whatever that cost. So he didn't say another word. He took it. He had to. Well, that's when I was 17, see? I'd been going through all this. That's why. And we couldn't make no money. I told you that, though, about making money to go to Canada. That's what I figured. You've got that. Well, the deal about actually clearing the land so you could plant a crop on it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, that land, when it was just bunch grass to start with, right?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Yeah. It was bunch grass. Bunch grass and sunflowers.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, what was the clearing of that land like?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: It was a prairie, but you had to plow it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you clear it?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Didn't clear nothing. Wait a minute. I'll tell you. Dad, he only had a 14-inch break in plow. And he had to borrow another Cayuse from Oscar Nelson to help to break this land, that is, the first year. And he couldn't break until in June when the grass was good because he had no hay. He had no grain. And he got the blacksmith to sharpen that shear. He said, don't make it hard. Make it soft so I can coal hammer it. You know what coal hammering is? So that he could have it just razor sharp to cut those great big sunflowers. They had roots this big. But he would plow, and he was smart enough to figure it out that he could go down deeper. But that made it hard for the horses to pull. But you couldn't hardly cut through the main crown. You had to go under it to get down to the tap root. And that's the way he struggled.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Then while his horses would eat, he'd turn the plow up and he'd take the hammer and maybe a wedge and sit there and sharpen it up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much could he clear?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, I don't know, that I can't remember. I know he plowed this 47 acres up, I think that one summer. And he just kept adding little by little every year, see, until he got it all broke. And then when us boys, see, you know, that's before mother died that I started plowing. I guess he got most of it broke up before she died. Let's see now. She died in 1901. He homesteaded in..… yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What year?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: 1896. He homesteaded in the year 1896. That's when you moved over there. That's when we moved over there. He had it pretty much broken up. Yeah, it took him about five years, you see.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what about you as a boy using that walking plow? Now that was rough work for a kid, wasn't it?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, like I told you, I was only 11 when I started out with it. It was up high here. But first time was a 14 inch plow and then finally got a new Canton Clipper plow, 16 inches.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A Canton?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: What they call a Canton Clipper. That's the name of it. And it scoured better. The 14 inch, being a 14 inch, that soil was sticky. Just that rich and it'd be sticky. So he got wise and got a 16 inch and the Canton Clipper seemed to scour better anyway. And then the bigger the plow, the better it scoured.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say scour, what do you mean by that?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, clog up… so it didn't plow, it just pushed the dirt. By golly. So he had me a plow. Well, way heck it'd be snow, foot snow around Christmas. I had to plow two or three months in the fall to get the ground plowed with only one plow, 165 acres. You can plow them short days about two acres a day. Them three Cayuses. That's kind of that. Well then...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You'd be working on this all day?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, it was only about six, seven hours, but I'd be out there that long steady. From nine o 'clock till three o 'clock is about all I'd work in them short days. But that's six hours and I didn't even get a lunch out there. That snow would be flopping down here on this leg from the side of the furrow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sounds like, that sounds for a kid, it sounds rough.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, I was 11 years old and I kept that up. He didn't get a gang plow till I was, like I said, I was about... Wait now, I've got to figure that out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well wait, you told me about the gang. You told me when you got ready for it, then you got it. Listen, I want to ask you something else about this, about his locating there. Now, you told me how he picked, where he picked and how he laid it out. Was he the first one in that vicinity?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No, he had a neighbor, Press Reagan and him. Press Reagan was coming from Park, he had a homestead in Park too. But Press Reagan and Dad, I guess must have located about the same time. Because then there was another fellow there, John Thomas' uncle, West Thomas. He located I think about the same time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they have to draw numbers?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No, it was thrown open, three homesteads. The first one first served. But I'll tell you one farmer there. Oh yes, I've got two or three I'm going to tell you about. Let's see, better start down on the ridge I guess first. The Rogers, his name was Ruben Rogers, that is the old man. And Mel Rogers was the son. And old Ruben Rogers, homesteaded, we'll say on the east side of Rasmussen. Rasmussen was a bachelor living out here on the breaks. And he took up a homestead. Mel Rogers took up 40 acres. No, wait a minute, he didn't take up, yes he did too take up 40 acres. Then old Ruben Rogers, well it would be a son-in-law, Ruben Rogers, that lived in Montana. He had a little money. He'd come down to homestead 80 acres. Right just across from the old man. And then the Hems, that was the Irish family, they had a homestead south of that again, southeast.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And right, that's another story I can tell you. I stood there when old Ruben Rogers, old Hem, the old husband was out just like my dad harvesting. And this old Ruben Rogers stood there and cussed this woman with all these children, had her crying, wanted her to move off of that party that they had, see it was close to their place. Tried to jump it. And you know what the farmers did then? They even built a cabin, I mean these Rogers had built a cabin on this party. Tried to jump it, don't you see? You know what the neighbors all did? They got cahootchers. One night, moonlight night, they took that cabin and rolled it down the hell side. That's how they treated them Rogers and they didn't get to jump that place. Hem stayed there and homestead it. See the rest of the farmers from there on up the ridge, they were organized.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And they also built this grade down where there wasn't any grade when we moved up there. About a three mile switch back grade down the Briggs Point we called it, right down over the ridge. They went along the hillside, just switched back and like that see, till they got down the bottom of the grade, or down the hill. Now they got together and did that as a... They got together and I'll tell you who was the cook. Mrs. John Center's, that's old man Center's wife was the cook. They built up a little cabin down there on what they called a saddle. Kind of a level spot, see, in this mountain. They built a cabin there. Because then they could go up, work up above the saddle and down below and come back there to eat. Evening, I guess they must have took a lunch along at noon. But everything was done hand work. Oh they built that, no wait a minute. I was so small I couldn't say how it... They must have had those great scrapers. Two horse scrapers like I told you I had to dig in the pond. That's about what they had.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That was the first road."

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh that's the first road they got. Well they didn't get the other new road till 1914. Because I worked on it. I was married then, see, I'd been married a year. No the farmers had... Well wait a minute, they had a contractor. Wait now I've got to think of who he was. Let's see. The contractor, he took a bid on that, building that new grade from the... Well it wasn't quite our corner, it was just about a half a quarter to the bricks from our place. It was on my uncle's, the place that my uncle bought, see. Right there they started and they went along this canyon side hill all the way down on the south side of this big canyon slope, see. All the way down. They made a, oh gosh they made a seven mile grade to go in there. Some of the people down at the lower end, they won't settle. He bought, he wanted to have it built close to the old grade, see.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He remodeled it, that's what he had figured.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How far was the old grade, how different was the old grade from the new one? What was the old grade?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well the old grade was the one that was switched back and see. Oh it was switched back, this one went just right down the side of the hill side. Well no, this was zigzagging along the following routine of the mountain. You had to go in, some coolies, out and around the ridges. It wasn't straight by any means, but you did an old switch by going down the hill like the other one. You know what I mean?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they keep up the old road after the new one?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, yeah, that was up to the people that lived on the lower end. And the Rogerses, just to show you, they stayed put. Well, Sinclair, see, he got so disgusted he finally just sold up and left. And the new guy was Dehmann, old, I thought the name of Dehmann.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why did Sinclair get disgusted?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Because he didn't think that while he was in debt a little bit, it was one trouble. He had a hard time making a go up. And his boy left him, he was plumbered along, he was a cripple, and so he damn near had to sell out. And Rogers, they played pretty cute. They got it for little or nothing. Well, they sicked another guy in there first, and they knew he couldn't make it, and they got it from him for little or nothing. And so now they own all that, well, damn, they're dead. Old man Rogers and his son is dead, but the grandson, Edgar, he's the boy that owns the whole works. From there on up, I guess they got to about four or five places. Clear up to our place. See, it's a narrow ridge. So that's the way it went. Well, now that's about all of that. Let me ask you about something else in there. The cabin, your father built the cabin. Well, just a little cabin to begin with, see.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That was the homestead cabin. And then he built, here, I'll show you a picture here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The Grandview Farm, did you call it Grandview?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Yeah, yeah, he named it that, yeah. Dad named it that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it a grand view?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: It was. Yeah, you could see Continent Butte way south. That's about 30 miles from where we lived. And you could see the Ball Mountain. What do you call this here? Big Potlatch Mountain? Yeah, we could see that in the clear day. Yeah, it was. Well, that's kind of high up there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, this little house that you lived in, the first one that he built, that wasn't very roomy, didn't have any...

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, we kids had to sleep up in the attic. They'd run up and down, he didn't even have a star, it was just a ladder. And I can tell you another little story there. While I lay in there, I got a toothache. Dad had went and... Let's see, yeah, he was an agent for this Japanese oil. And he'd been doing pretty good selling it. He said, there's one old Dutch woman, didn't believe it was any good, see. Well, he said, it's just strong enough, he said, you put it on your skin, he says, it'll burn you. Well, she took her tongue out and he just... She got the call and she had to get some water. Well, that's what I could tell you. That was very good for two things. If you could hold it in your mouth a little while, or put it on your ... That's all you had to do, really. And I lay there asleep, I tried to pull the score. I pulled it out, all right, it'd come in this eye. Boy, I run down that ladder, and I run around this log house here, hollering for dad to help me. I said, I've got a Japanese oil in my eye, there's this eye. Right eye. Oh, he said, he was groggy and sleepy, he says, I've got a fit. I said, listen, daddy, it's Japanese oil in my eye.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I said, I had the two things, I tried to get in my mouth, I said, I was sleepy, and pulled the cork out. He understood I was just a ..., I was just as crazy as I could be. He got up and got me some water, and I started washing, and I finally got it out. Boy, that was one good time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, your mother, you said before she died she was sick for a while.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, she was, dad had sent her to Spokane to find out what the trouble was to a specialist. And he shouldn't have told her, but he said, the doctor told her that she had TB, and wasn't going to live long. He told her that, right to her face. She says, well, I have time enough to get home to see my family. Oh, yes, he says, you might live six months, eight months, maybe a year, he says, if you take care of her. Well, she lived, I think, let's see. Let's see, he was up there, yes, she died, not quite a year. He was up there in the spring, the spring before she died, February 22nd. About ten months, I guess, she lived.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That last year, did she still try to work and do everything?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, boy, that gave her what they call scotch emulsion. That was supposed to cure TB. And she'd drink that, but it didn't help her. She was too far gone. And she'd cough up, I guess it kind of loosened up this stuff. I seen that poor mother of mine just strangled sometimes, tears come out of her eye, and she'd just be all exhausted and fall over. You'd think she'd died. That's how bad she was.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think it was much rougher for her living in a little cabin than it would have been?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, all them old parts. She wasn't the only one died on them prayers. Mrs. Hardman was another one that died with TB, and Mrs. Tetler was another one that died with TB. It's like this cousin of mine was here visiting her and her brother and their husbands. And this young, she kind of dumbs, she says, when I said mother didn't live quite to be 32. She would have if she lived till May. She'll act from February till May being 32. That'll be February, March, April, May, about three months, being 32. So I took her over here. I said, look. I said, look here now. Here's the bedroom. This chicken, dad moved it for a chicken house that he attached onto that log cabin I showed you. On the west side. And I said, us kids wasn't big enough to cut wood. I said, dad had to do it all. And I said, that's all the heat she had was that wood stove.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: How would you like to live in a thing like that being sick? And he warmed her feet by putting bricks in the stove, either bricks or flat arms by her feet to keep her feet warm. And how do you like to let light back and pull through it… oh, shut up… i'm proud of my parents. I said, boy, these are just the most honorable ones I ever dreamt of. I said, this is my dad here. And dad knew it too, but of course he kind of favored me then I guess he did. He didn't do too much favoring. He kind of, I'm glad he didn't. He made us kids get out and dig. Now he helped that uncle there, and he helped another one, Sigwart, that went east. Same as give him $700, he was going to go back there. Of course, Sigwart made good though. He went back there and got educated. See, that was the thing in them days. Nobody got educated.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: But he went back there. He was a horse man. He went back there and he got married. The woman had a little money, and she put him through veterinary school. And he became a veterinarian back in North Dakota, I think it was, North or South Dakota. And he made good. As far as I know, he never did pay dad back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So your dad, he was more likely maybe to give money to his brothers than to his kids.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Yeah, he helped them out more than he did us kids. Oh, he helped me. No, I won't say he didn't help me. The first year I was married, we didn't get only, we got a, well, he'd done this for me. Before I got married, I was so insect that they're on the reach for this settler boy. He had a thrashing machine and he run these death thrashing machine. And this Bob Thompson come down there. He heard that. You see our name is all over the prairie. And they knew who was to be depended on who what. And one reason was dad had been that insurance. I told you about that fire insurance man. And so he got well acquainted and they figured from that that he was an honest guy that children would be pretty good. So this old Bob Thompson come down there and he'd seen me work. I was on sacks. He was beat to death. Of course, I was 25 then, a young man, a husky. Coming over to where I was at and he said, I guess the machine stopped a little or something happened that he had a chance to talk a little. Maybe it's noon hour. I don't remember.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He says, hey, I'm looking for a young couple. He says, I understand you're going to get married this fall. Yeah. He says, I'd like to hire, or he says, I'd like to go have you go in partnership with me for cattle. Well, I kind of darn near wanted to buy half in. See, dad took me out of that trap. Don't you do it. He said, I've heard he knew something about this guy. See, you better get acquainted. He said, you better live there for a year first. We're cheap for the first year, but a month. She put $40, $45 a month for both of us and both, which we did. I put it up to her myself. I'm a missus. I'll work for you for $45 and both. And I had already bought my stove, just a cook stove, wood stove, and some furniture and bedding. And I'd made that much money that I was able to do that much. And I told him that. Well, that's just what he wanted. See, somebody that was kind of equipped.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And he bought a, he had a ticket for a place over, that's on the mountainside too, over there on Angel Ridge side, just up from Peck, about three or four or five miles. And about four or five miles down to Leno, they call it. It's all on the hillside, but he had a bench land, see what I mean, with springs on it. He thought he was going to go into cattle, don't you see, where it's cheap land. He got that land cheap. And it was just a shanty, just one bold shanty that we lived in. And so, he agreed to pay for it, and he did pay $45 a month. We got our money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he have a house there of his own besides or did he?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, no, just, no, we all lived in the same house with him. He ate with us. My mess was cooked for him, see. That's what he wanted. So that was the work she did for him. She cooked. That was it. She was a housekeeper. And I was to do this plowing and hauling hay and whatnot. And go out, if he bought cattle, help him get the cattle home. So, now here's an incident I'm going to tell you. We borrowed a sled from a neighbor up Dike. Wait, I guess that was his name. Wait, no, it's similar to it. Dykes was his name. Dykes. And that was a good sled. We made it all right. But one time you had to buy hay from Springstons up on Angel Ridge. We had to go up a mountain to get to their place where the hay was. And they had the bob sled. But it had a big hole in the front bolster with a king bolt, see, and it just rocked, just like a rocking chair.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And Springstons told us, they said, you can have that sled, but look out, it'll tip over on flat ground. Well, that's the only thing Bob could see. And he had an overcoat on. We'd got the hay on. We had a pole on it, loose hay, tied at both ends. And of course, I'd drive in the four horses, Cayuse as they were. We started down this mountain, we didn't have no rough lock on it. Just a little bit of snow, but they'd be rock. It had hit rock once in a while. And I'd kind of slow it up. And I could feel that thing rocking. And old Bob was sitting behind, or in the middle of the sled, hay, lone, with two forks like this, with these overcoats on. I was young as he'd carried me. I stepped over here to the edge. I said, Bob, I said, you'd better get back to the end there, this thing's going to tip. You'd see chuck holes now and then. God almighty, I just knew it wasn't. And I couldn't make the horses go slower. They were just plopping. All of a sudden, bingo, she went. And I jumped. Bob flipped. I hit the front bob, but I lit. Accidentally, it didn't happen to hit me in the crotch. I jumped off, I was caddy, and I jumped off to the side, and I was still holding the horses. And I tied them to the sled. This whole load of hay rolled down, and it just so happened about A yellow pine tree about four foot in diameter, about as far down as to this barn. Right down a bunch of shale rock. And old Bob was shoved all the way down.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He laid right square under the middle of that load of hay. And I could hear him. He says, get me out, get me out. Yes, Barrett can hear you. He's clear under the middle. Well, I said, you got both the forks. I said, I'm going to go. Well, I was excited, and he did tell me that. He says, you better cut the rope. Get the pole off. Well, that did let the sled, the rack back. And I pawed it with my hands… got him out… you know what happened to him? He broke three ribs for his smartness trying to tell me what to do, and he didn't listen to me. So I got to tell you more about that guy. That's quite a trip we had there. So then, oh, he couldn't help me. I had to carry all that hay up and haul it home myself… i got carried… i don't remember how long it took me, but I had to get that hay carried up. We had to have the hay at home. We couldn't do as good down the hillside.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You mean you didn't have no sled then?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, the sled was up there, but I had to get the hay up to the sled. Tip! Hell, I was in a fire. I said to the barn, I had to climb that shale of rock with that hay to get up there. And then, when I got just in the gate, last gate to where we lived by the barn, the damn thing tipped over again. That's the last time we used that sled. I said, Bob, I won't go with that sled no more. I said, now the next load, I want that other sled. And he couldn't help me. I had to go up the mountain and go over to Springsteen to get that load of hay myself. But I was glad of it. I felt the downside better off. I had to work a little harder to get the load on maybe.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did this guy have enough land to raise cattle?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He went broke. You needed a lot of land to raise cattle. Well, he had no. He only had 15 or 20 head of cattle. He was a dumb nut. The old wheat farmer. He thought he ran his wheat land up there by the mower. Thought he'd make enough to keep this other going, I guess, to tie them all away. I can tell you, this wasn't all just beef. It was kind of a new purpose, because he was selling little cream to pay us… for staying there… well, God, the cream didn't bring much money. He'd get maybe one can of five-gum can of cream a week. He had all that clear to pack. Five, six miles. And then in the spring, when it come to planting this corn, I plowed up some Timothy sod for him. He wanted that plowed to put in the corn. So he made a marker. You know, to plant the corn in. Roll, if you understand. He made a marker. And I had one with two horses. Didn't need more than two horses to pull this marker. So he says, I'll go to Peck with a can of cream.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: You take the two and mark that corn ground. I said, okay. Well, he hadn't made it quite right. It was running along the nose, and it would jump around, see, on this bad ground. So I stood on it, behind to hold it down. Well, of course, that made it tough going for the horses. Two-coyote. I couldn't do much. I had to puff them, rest them. And he'd come back long in the afternoon. That was in the spring season. That's what started the fugitive misunderstanding between us. So he said, why didn't you put a rock on? Well, he put a rock on. Didn't work very good. He had to change the hitch. I told him it wouldn't work. I said it had to be just about my weight to hold it down. He found it out. He had to change that hitch on there. You see, now, he'd have to, I think, I don't remember now, which way he'd change it, but he had to change it.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Anyway, one cow he bought was a great big ..., see. And she's supposed to be a kicker. And he was sitting over there milking on one side of the barn, and I was over here. And when he said that she was a kicker, I just kind of was curious. And I was sitting there looking, you know, watching my milking away, but I'd look to see. All of a sudden, that cow just reached up with her hind foot. If he'd had her in the stance, it'd have been fine, but he had a long chain, and she had room to back up, see. And she backed up enough, she got her hind foot up here just as clever as could be, kicked him back like that. And just as he went, she'd give him another kick right in the rear. And I was laughing. Oh, I could have died. I didn't dare. I was afraid he'd get mad at me, see. I seen he was a spunky guy. He was a man by 65 then. And I was only a young buck, 25, you know. He had a cream separator, and he'd turn in that cream separator, I'd come in there. I said, Bob, you don't know how bad I wanted to laugh out there when I seen that cow kick you. He was good natured then.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, yeah, he had made this remark. He wasn't supposed to whip cows, see. Made him so damn mad, he picked that stool up, I said, boy, you do turn into that cow to beat the nasty. I said, boy, and he said, he was a hucky old devil. He had a good big heavy neck, and he was compact built, you know… stooled he built… so he pushed her up against the wall, and that's how he killed her. Pretty good. He didn't get much milk out of him. They claimed, you know, when you fight a cow, she'll hold the milk.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did you stay with him for very long?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, not a whole lot then. Here's another thing that happened. He had a daughter going to Normal, down at Lewis, Normal. She'd come up there, along in the street after we guys, after we got the planting all done. And she was only a kid about, oh, around 16, I think, or 17, along in there. Going to that Normal school at Lewiston. Going to try to be a school mom, I guess. So these ponies was all out in the pasture, you know, grazing. And she had a girlfriend come there with her from Lewiston. She ordered me to go get these ponies up and saddle them up. I guess Bob had a saddle or he barred some. I don't remember that, but he had saddles. He wanted me to saddle these ponies up so that they could go take a ride… i said, okay… i went and got them, saddled them up, brought them up there. And they got on, took a ride, and then they come back. They just dropped the reins, and well, the horses took out in the pasture. And I didn't know nothing about it until they were gone, see. Then she started fussing at me. I got to go catch them ponies. I said, Jesus Christ, I caught them once. I said, it's your turn now to get them. I was about ready to balk in over there, and I thought, God damn, they're going to order me around here like this. They're going to get fooled.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So, of course, saddles, what about the old man?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That made him pretty, I don't know, maybe they planned it that way, too. By God, I stayed with my ideas. And, well, he said, I guess I can't afford to keep you people. I said, that's fine. I said, I'm ready to quit anyway. So, Dad, of course, that's why I said Dad helped me. He knew I had furniture up there, and he had friends at Peck. He got a place to store our furniture, but he had no room at home. So, he come over with a forest wagon, and he got target with old Tawson C. Dad told you all. No wonder he used to raise hogs up in the motor seat. He said, no wonder they called you Hog Thompson up there. Oh, Dad was a good man. Boy, he did answer Dad's questions. I tell you, Dad was pretty spoiled. Yeah, well, he was just a thief. Fourteen? Yeah, how old was Dad then? Oh, hell, he was only forty-something.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He was nobody's fool. He was no weakling. He could have taken care of the old Tawson all right. Tawson was at least sixty, maybe sixty-five. And he was too catty. He was kind of a muscle bound. He was pretty husky, but he wasn't near as good a man as he thought he was. So, that led to that. Well, then, that was fourteen. 1914, see, that this happened. Because this was the first winter that we were married. There were nineteen, thirteen, and fourteen. Well, then that fall of fourteen is when this new grade was being built. And I got this job down there, two bits an hour, ten hours, two and a half.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You had to do it?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: For this, from this contractor.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do on the grade?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Huh, pick and shovel, please. And I and my uncle, the one that married my aunt, Al Stamper, we didn't do nothing about digging rocks. See, you were supposed to move one whole rod of hillside, rocks included, and everything ten foot. Make a ten foot wide grade. One rod in ten hours. Well, we was up there scratching like little chickens. We didn't get no place. Just happened to be an elderly man there, one that had worked in the army. He knew how. He come over to us boys, nice old fellow, smiled and said, Hey, you boys working too hard. Well, he says, what do you do? We're trying to get this much dirt out. Well, yeah, but he says, you can't do it that way. He says, look at me. He says, I'm digging underneath. He says, it'll come to you. Dig underneath and it'll come to you. Boy, after that we had it easy.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That's just what it did. All you had to do was dig in and undermine it and that dirt would, maybe one lick or two would make it come… see… hell, we just, after that we got going fine. Got a long swell. And we was boarding at this house, because this camp was in this house that I moved for a hog house that Dad had bought. See, from this Skelton here. The place there where the...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You were boarding at, was it a Skelton's place at that time?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No, no, no, no. No, this, uh, this Skelton house is the one I moved over for a hog house. And, uh, but that, that was before I moved to see. That was when I was, 1914, when I was about coming 26, when I worked on that new grade. And we had to walk up for half a mile. Well, I guess we took our lunch at noon, but night and morning, see, we had to walk up the hill to get up to this place to eat. And of course I went over home to sleep. in a way, wait now, let's see. We were working there like that and a fellow from, my uncle and I, we got to talking. The job was about petered out. We were putting you through with it… long there… we weren't worrying about a winter job. Talk, you know a man will talk. Or it happened to be a fellow from the powder man, in other words. One that was doing all the blasting. And, uh, he was there and he says, boys, he says, why don't you come up to Orofino and get a woodcutting job.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what kind is it?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: We got curious… what kind of a job is it? Well, he says, and who do we get it from? He said, go up there to go, no, wait a minute, John Mix was the name. Go up there and see John Mix. He does hiring of the men to cut this wood on that place or his place. And he said, you got to go up three miles from Orofino to the job. But they've got a log cabin up there. Big log cabin that you live in. Well, I and the wife was young and no kids then. We was free. But here's the deal. I was sympathetic for my uncle and his three little kids my aunt had. They were just getting starved. They're living over here at a Park with ... on a rented place and them poor little kids standing in rags. And I felt so sorry for them. And I had a little few dollars saved up to see from this other job. I said, Al, he says, how can I get over there?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I said, Al, by God, don't worry. I said, I'll see if you can get over there. I said, we'll hire some guy over there. There was a fellow named Bill Jellaberg in the Park. He had a good team. I said, we can throw in whatever we need to get over there. Well, I'm getting a little ahead. This fellow, when he said cutting wood, I said, how can you make money doing that? I said, what kind of wood? He said, red fir, most of it. And he said, that don't freeze up. It'll split right in the dead of winter. But he said, the yellow pine, stay away from that. He says, that'll freeze up. Well, I said, OK. So we agreed to be partners, to go up there. And I got this Bill Jellaberg to haul us over there. Well, I got a little too far. He said, how can you get a big yellow pine tree? How the hell would you open it up?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, that's where he was smart. You see, he could handle powder. He says, I can just stick a little dynamite in there and open it up. He says, cut a log maybe 20 foot long and open it up. Place a quarter of it or half of it into wherever I want to saw it. And he says, the rest of it will split pretty good with a wedge. Well, that was all new. I was just off of a green farm, you know, just been raising wheat and choring for dad. It's all new. But by God, I had the guts. I went up there, moved my uncle up there. And it was a two-story affair. This cabin was two-story. And so I said to my uncle and aunt, I said, you live below. I said, you've got the family. We can climb the stairs and live up above. And the farmers would bring pork in there, 100-pound pigs, for $4, $4 or $5, a whole hundred, them days, cheap. Everything was cheap, you know.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: But you eat, boy, when you cut wood and in the cold weather, you could eat like a pig, you know. I bought, I don't know, two or three of them small pigs. They were nice and tender. So your wife was with you and you lived upstairs. Oh, yeah. But we had to get our groceries. At first, before he got the job of hauling wood, we had to walk to Orofino, three miles down the back of six miles. We had a pack sack on our back to carry our groceries, believe it or not. And I bought a six and a half foot Simon saw. And I hadn't learned to file it. I bought two, but I still got them. And so I didn't know how. I cut my drags too much. For one man, you can't do that. It worked pretty good for when Al and I was sawing together. But when he was a teamster, he'd been on the farm and he just loved to drive horses. The old mix, he wanted one of us to deck this wood out to where they could shove it down the hill to a flume.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And Al says, oh, I can't quit you. He says, you brought me over here. No, Al, I said, if you'd rather have that, you like horses and he's got to move that wood. I said, does that work good for him? Everything will be hunky dory. I said, I'll learn how to cut by myself… don't worry… but then it just so happened there were two woodcutters that knew the business. I mean, the filing the saw. They had a little saw, five and a half foot saw. They wanted to trade with me. And I tried to sell. Well, I could see that that would be no good because it didn't have the weight. I said mine was stiff too and it was a little limber. I told him, I said, how do you file a saw? I said, so it'll cut better for one man. Oh, he said, you got the drags too short. You've just got to cut that out. And I said, look, the Thursday wood wasn't as short as mine.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He said, well, I said, how do you gauge that? Well, you've got to have a gauge. And he set that. He's a little set group. See, I've got it yet. You set that and about the thickness, he said, don't cut them off. But for one man in the winter like that, when it's frozen timber or hard timber like red fur, about the thickness of a newspaper or not more than the playing card. And Jesus, I got good at it. I got so I could fix it, you know, and I'd swedge it to cut it. The drags a little bit so they'd grab it. And these are quite, they just plane it right out. And I got good enough that I could file my own timber. I'd cut me a little sapling with a little twig like that to lay my back on my sawing. I'd start in over here. If I wanted to fall that tree, we'll stay over there. Well, I'd hold it. Wait a minute. No. If I wanted to fall that tree here, I would cut it off over here. And then I'd hold it here so she'd go where I wanted. I kept going on around. When I thought it was enough, about two or four inches, it didn't go.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I'd put a wedge in and make a gulf where I wanted. And that's just why I had luck when I was working in the woods. Here's a picture of me that had come back out of the woods. That's 1936. Oh, you told me about 1936. And we got these pictures. Now look, I look pretty husky there. You sure do. Well, by God, I'd cut about 40 acres of timber. I had three partners. Yeah, you told me about 1936. But you worked this time in Orofino by yourself then. Oh, yeah, in Orofino. I worked after he got the wood driving, I mean, teaming job. I worked by myself.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How much did you cut by yourself?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I'd cut… good days, when I was feeling good, I'd make two cords a day… four foot… you didn't cut it in 16 inch, but just four foot. But just the same, you had to split it all and you had to deck it down on a... If your tree was up here in the mountain, you had to roll it down here to the flat where you could get at it with a team. Had to do a little extra.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the fellow with the dynamite? Did he work with you at all?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No, no, we didn't see him no more. Oh, no. No, I don't know what he'd done. You know, you're talking about these first years when you were married, and I was wondering how you met your wife. How you met her and how... Oh, I met her. I'll tell you, when I first met her, that was out here in the Endicott country. You know where Endicott, Washington is?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Endicott, Washington is? Where is it near? What else is out there beside Endicott?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, you know where Colfax is? Well, you go about south... Wait a minute. No, you go north. Northwest to get to Endicott. Then they sell what they call Dusty, but you don't go that far. I know that, sure. Well, you don't go that far. Endicott...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you working in the harvest or what?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, wait. You see, these... I went to this school, agriculture school here at Moscow University. And I met a guy, I got a picture there, Haley Jones. And that was winter before... You see, that was in 19... Wait a minute. Yeah, that was 1913. See, I was 1912 and 13, and I worked at Bovill in logging woods. Then when spring came, I didn't want to stay up there and invite fires in the woods. I just didn't like it. I'd had enough fire experience on a little Moscow fire, and I just knew more of that. So this Haley Jones, he says, Helmer says, why don't you come down to Endicott? He says, work for my brother. He's got a big farm. And he said, he hires men, and quite a few. And he said, there's a lot of girls, a lot of pretty girls down there. That's what he said. Which it was. Well, I was young, you know, I thought, okay, boy, that's the place for me.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And it was nice. They had a church there, you know. I'd go to church. And this other guy that was working with me, I got a job for his brother. And this kid that was working with him, with me, on that place, his name was Brocke, 17-year-old kid. And he went to church with me, you know. And I just happened to spot this, my wife it was. I didn't tell you. I'd been going with this, these guys' sister, too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Brocke's sister?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: No, no, no, no. The man I worked for. And the one I went to school with, see. They were brothers. And I went to school. So I went to do her out for a buggy. I'd hired a buggy team. Just out for being friendly, you know, because she was a sister to the boys. But she's only 17. And oh, there was a lot of pretty girls there. Jesus Christ, they were one of them flirting to beat hell. She was, really, I thought I'd dined it, but she was a slicker, too. You had to watch out. You knew them slickers. They played dirty tricks on you. The way I found that out, you know, you buy, they had these masquerade, no, no, wait a minute. They had ice cream socials-like at church, see. And you're supposed to pick out a partner and treat them. And so I and this banker's daughter, that became the friend of my wife. She was only 16 and she was a little flirt and she was cute. She said, I want to go with you down to, what was it, we had to get something. Then she had to go into her dad and he was a banker, see. I seen him smiling to me. Oh, it was a little, he was hauling on a little wagon, I think it was. I'd hauled her there on that seat. He was laughing over that.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I don't know what he thought, but I didn't give a damn. I got back, you know. So this other girl that was so pretty, she wanted me to buy her something to eat. I don't remember if I did, but I found out she was a tricker. You know, so, what the hell was that noise? I think maybe she did. I bought a little something, she went and ate with somebody else, see. You know what I mean? That settled it with me. Well then I got acquainted. No, I didn't get acquainted yet with my wife, see. Oh, I got acquainted, yeah, that is, no, no, I didn't either. Because when I went to church with this young kid, Brocke kid, and I seen her up there, she was dressing white and she was in the singing choir, see, singing. Her dad was a preacher, my God, he's picture here. Her dad was a minister preacher of that church.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And I said to Brocke, he said, I said, who's that girl dressed in white? I said, that's our preacher's daughter, God allowed you. I said, God just didn't allow her to touch you, son. And her dad, when I was going, I even brought this other girl to church, don't you see, or this. And the old man, he got a kid of me. He told me to get out here to the door to say Kansas… you go now… well, sir, he says, there's a time in a young man's life, he said, that you like to be around a young lady's, ain't it? Oh, I said, I answered him quick. I said, oh, I said, you experienced that too, have you? Oh, yes, he said, many, many years ago. Well, I didn't know then that he had a daughter, see. So then by golly, she, this wife, she got a job out the same dang ranch where I worked in the cook house to cook for the men during harvest, see. And we was in the hay then, and I was hauling hay. And this other girl that I'd been going with, she was there, and they was both of them standing there yacking at me, and I had a Jackson fork, you know, to set in the hay. And I could show you that scar yet. I went right, one time, went right down the top of my shoe and into my ankle bone.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What's this, you weren't paying very good attention to your work?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, the girls were talking, I was trying to talk and work too, see. Two girls to answer. Oh, so then, I didn't say I worked, see, that hurt so bad.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And finally they asked, what's the matter?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I said, oh, God, I said, I went and had a dog gone forked down my shoe, and I got my shoe off, and I couldn't, it just pained me so bad. I couldn't, well, I finished that load, but I didn't do no more. This man, brother to this girl I was going with, you see, Jones, he had a one-horse buggy. So he said, well, take that buggy and horse and go into the doctor. So I did. Well, then on, well, I got a coin to the old op-air at the ranch, that's right. She was cooking, see, and she'd come out and play it a little bit, and the evening after supper, see, we had, the farmer had a swing, a swing. So I'd swing her, don't you see. And I got, I kind of got, she talked pretty interesting too to me across the table. Jesus Christ, that's the one I believe I thought I would have. And I thought I'd find out anyway.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: So she finally said after I swung her, well, I said, I've got to hurry and go do the dishes. I said, how about me helping, see. Yeah, you can help if you want to. I said, okay, that's fine, see, that's what gives me the chance. And I had a jump problem, you know. I said, what can I do to help? Oh, you can watch the dishes, okay. Then I approached her. I said, how would you like to correspond with me? She says, I don't play no second fiddle. She goes, oh, that's so good. I said, you don't have to. I said, you play first fiddle, if you say so. That started the whole thing. Well, then it just seemed like everything was cut out. See, I got hurt. I had to go to town to see that doctor every so often. And because I couldn't work, I was laid up. That foot was sore. And he put a gut string, opened it so it would drain.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He wanted me to come in so he could keep it open and see that it was draining good. The gut is right on the ankle bone, you know, particularly his place. Well, then on a Sunday, she was free. And we went out buggy riding in this single buggy, see, after I'd seen the doctor. And the doctor and his family was out car riding. And we were sitting there spooning. And so when I come in there to pay the doctor, the doctor says, how much you owe me? Well, he said, I'll tell you. He said, I got about $10 worth of scenery out there spooning. He said, I'll just make it $10. We like to never hurt the last of them. Well, then she got to working on this farm, you see. And she got a job for a fellow, Macham, which is his name, about five miles. And this banker's daughter and her was the cooks for that, he was a bachelor for that man. And so every Sunday I'd get this spooning right out there, see, just here. And I think that was after we were engaged, though. It wasn't too long. I didn't think it was over a month after I started going with her until we got engaged. Well, a correspondent isn't the same as engaged.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A correspondent is just going with her, right?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Yeah, to start with. Oh yeah, we were engaged while we was out there on the Jones Place. I took her into town on a Saturday evening when she was going to be at home on Sunday. And I approached her kind of odd. I said, I guess there's a gate down on the farm's place. I said, how do you like that? What do you think? If that was our gate, we were going through like that. And she talked favorably to me. Well, something hung in my head. The old man, after I got to going with her, he kind of was quiet. I said, well, I don't know. I said, you know about your old man? I said, he cares for me. She said, that don't make any difference as long as I... Well, I thought that's right, too… see… well, heck, I'd have married him. If she was feeling like that, well, that was what I wanted. That's the kind of answer I wanted. God damn it. I liked the young fellow. I thought I'd already overstepped. I thought I'd said too much.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: You know, it's kind of a shock to a young fellow. First time you approach somebody like that, you know, you're used to that kind of answer. But I don't know. Nothing. I loved her. God willing. Well, just to show you, there's our 50th anniversary plate. And here's some more presents we got right in here. Well, she lived 54 years, 3 months and 6 days after we was married. And raised that big family.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Helmer did..… her father was a preacher, right?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh yeah, he was a United Methodist preacher. Oh sure, he's pictured just so you can get an idea.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Going to church together every Sunday?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, she was working out there at the farm, you see. That other farm. And I went there. But then, when this harvesting was done on that place, I went to the central ridge. To get another job. And that's where I had this saxophone job. That's when that old Thompson came down there, you understand what I told you, I got that job. That's where I was married. Oh, wait, wait. When I asked him, see. I asked him alright. I said, I'm just going to let it pass by without saying something. So I told Ethel, we sat beside each other and the old man out there crossed from us. I said, Mr. Geisler, have you got any objections to me and Ethel getting married this fall? He's kind of wise. He says, well, no. He says, I haven't. He says, have you got any work lined down the seat like that? Well, I'd worked in the woods the winter before.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, I said, I think I can get work back. I'm not sure. But I think I can get back up in the woods. I worked up there last winter. I said, I made it pretty good then. Well, alright, he said. But I didn't go back to the woods. Got this other job. I'll tell you, in the woods in the winter, it's pretty bitter, you know. Well, I had to bend away from her. Getting this job together on the farm was a whole lot nicer, you see, being first year married. I've come to get that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what do you think? Now, do you want to know?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Wait a minute. Now, that's all of that. But I was going to tell you how I got lined up to buy, to get me a home.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You want to know that?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, wait a minute. I'm not done, really. Oh, okay. Asking you about that when you were first married. Because to me, that's a time that's really important in a person's life. Yeah, well, okay. And I'm wondering how you found it to be, what it was like to be newlywed in those days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How was it when you were first married? In those days, did you and your wife get along without any disagreements?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, yeah, we just loved one another fine. I'll tell you. Yeah, 19... I got there some more. 1915, that was two years after we was married, see. Now, remember, 1915. My dad went to my note to buy a team to farm Oscar Nelson Place, that is 65 acres of it. And we were supposed, she was supposed to keep house there. And I'm out in the field working, see. And I had to go in debt for that team, see. I didn't have no money. And I didn't really want to go in debt. I mean, to buy the team, gee, it cost over $300 to buy that team. And I had to buy a feed and seed to keep the horses and to keep the seed to farm, don't you see. And I told dad, I don't know about it. Well, he says, that's pretty good land. He said, you might get a good crop. He said, better he gave him to let me try it. He'd come back to my note. I said, okay.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: So we got it. I bought seed, oats, what we put it into, from a fellow named Press Reagan. Gave him a dollar and a half a bush, or no, a hundred. And when fall came, I did, I was just lucky enough to have a good crop of oats. We had got the ground work good. And we went along fine until, well, when I was a plowman, of course, I didn't go to the fine. I better tell you that, I guess. Old Oscar, he, dad says, now, he says, I got my plowing done. He says, you can get this gang plow and four horses from me so he can get the ground plow quicker, see. This old Swede, he's a bullheaded old devil. I took his advice that time. He'd come over there, well, that's where this Gilbert, I'm telling you about that Uncle Gilbert, he was hard up. He was farming another place then down there, but he was hard up.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And he'd got around this Oscar Nelson scene, talked him into making me hire him. Because I had to use him to do the drilling, because dad was busy drilling his own. And so he'd come and he said, get him to not use this gang plow, just make him use a walking plow. And he had to, that way I had to hire him. The Oscar says, well, you can get Gilbert Swenson to come and help you. With two 16 inch plows, it'll go just as fast or faster, which, of course, that other gang was 14. But here was the deal. He thought a walking plow would go deeper. But he was a man of one of these growing plows, deep in the spring of the year, mind you. Crazy ideas, what it was. Well, he'd come and check me on a corner where it was clay. Well, there you can't make any plow go down very deep. And that's when he said he'd split down the, made me quit. I had to take all the dad's gang plow home, the other four horses home, and get that going Gilbert. Well, then I'll tell you how we wound up.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: When fall came, I'd been out, John Shod was running the thrashing machine. He'd done the thrashing for me. And I'd run my teeming bundle wagon in so much a day. And my wife is still in the house with this bachelor cooking, see. And she was baking bread one day. And the phone rang. They had, he had a phone. He had a carton to work in there… there's another suite… and he had a carton working there. So she had to cook for him and this bachelor too, see. And he was building, you know, he had a spring down there and he wanted to get, he had dug a hole, but he wanted some buildings put up over it. So it'd be sanitary. And kind of a tank, I guess. Yeah, it was down low. He could run the water into it, see, and make it more water. He didn't want to be hauling, doing the harvest. You had to get farmers, I mean, you had to furnish water for steam engines. And he didn't want to bother his neighbors.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He didn't hitch too good with his neighbors over water. And then, of course, they had to go about two or four miles to get it too. So, my golly, he, wait now. The phone rang when she had her hand in the bread. She says, Oscar, would you mind going answering that phone? He says, Ethel, I told you to go answer that phone. What she says, Oscar, I've got my hand full of bread dough. She says, they're ringing. And he stomped the phone like that. Ethel. God, once he told me that, boy, that made my blood boil. Oh, God, I said, I can't hardly wait until I can get a hold of that son of a bitch. And yet, you had to be careful not to hit that old bastard. He's eyes just danced in his head. You know, he couldn't see good. Yet, he was a man who could play five or six instruments. He knew music. And he could read if he'd take a book up like this.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I'd be god darned if he couldn't read, but he had to hold it close. But it made me so then, I had worked for that bastard when I was a kid. Well, I mean before I'd married. Pitching bundles for three wagons for him. And he had, he ran stallions. He had three stallions. And he worked two of them on a wagon. That time that he was hauling, one of them got kind of slow, I guess, or kind of trying to balk. That was a big black old shire. And he took the fork like that to hit him, see. And he finally made it up the hill. And what he had claimed was, and that's the story I started to get his attention. See, I told Settle, I said, I don't want to hit that old bastard if I don't have to. And I said, you're a good witness. But you stay there. You just watch and listen to what's said. I said, I'm going to try and bring it up slow. And I said, in case I hit him.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He had a lot of lawsuits with guys, you know, just trucking. I didn't want nothing like that. But I thought if I did too bad I might hit him anyway. So Settle said, he agreed. Settle was a friend of mine. He hated him too. He said, yeah, he's a stubborn old devil. I said, he's going to admit it. I said, I'm going to slap the hell right out of him. So I said, Oscar, you know you claimed you didn't never tell... No, first it started out, how you telling about Charlie Coon and Gilbert… that's my uncle… well, he was rough on horses. And he didn't believe in that licking horses. I said, that's what you said, Oscar, that you didn't believe in. No, Settle, he said, he stood up like this, you know. No, Settle, he said, don't believe in licking horses. I said, Oscar, you know something? I said, by God, I said, one time I hauled hay with you for you pitching in the field. You had an old black tunnel. I said, he bought it. I said, you took a goddamn pitch Park. I said, and you started licking him with that. I said, if that ain't licking, I like it a lot.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: That's when I never said, you mean to call me a liar? I put my sleeve up to my elbow and I walked right up close to him and he stood there like this. I met it. I said, you bastard, I said, you told my wife too. I said, the other day. By God, I said, you ain't talking sass, and neither one of us from now on. I said, we're through. And, well, he said, your grandpas won't like that. I said, they never bought my bread. I said, by God, I knew what they are. I said, don't worry. I said, I'm not worrying about it. I tried to work on my conscience. Jesus Christ, I knew where I stood. I knew my grandpas. They wouldn't pay attention to a bull headed like him. And they didn't either. But anyway, he had bought just to show you. He figured strong on getting us for the next year because he'd already bargained the neighbor.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He wouldn't let you cut hay on his place, in other words.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He wouldn't let me cut hay off of that crop for the next year. I had to buy it from a neighbor. That's how stubborn he was. He wanted to be sure he got the third exactly in trashing deal, don't you see?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I'm not sure I see because he wouldn't let you cut his hay.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He would let me cut hay on his place for my horses. I had to buy it from somebody else. He wanted all his crop thrashed. So he could get a third of the thrashed grain, you see.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was trying to get every nickel out of you.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, maybe somebody... No, but he just got that idea in his head. And he'd been getting rented, but they kept quitting him because he was a damn stubborn, see. He had one rent... I was the second one on that same place.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did you leave right away then?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, no. The way nobody got to do the harvest wasn't over. You betcha. ... ... the kind of qualities that you were looking for, that you saw in your wife, that you didn't see in other young women. You know, what was it you were looking for that she had that other women... Well, honesty. Honesty. Truthful. And she was brought up with Christianity in her soul. See? All my people, my grandparents, my parents, all of them belonged to the Lutheran Church. Come from the old country, they all was church people. Over here at the Park where Steiner is, them Lutherans all built a church, Lutheran Church. And I can remember when my granddad and grandma would come there to church when we were little kids over there. They'd come there, I guess, well whenever they had preaching there, see? There was a preacher by the name of Andreas. He was a Lutheran preacher. And later on, it became there was another one. They were a nice couple. They were more, you might say more modern. They were ... He had a job in Deary and then he'd go to Park.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Those little country places every so many Sundays. I don't know just how he had it arranged. But they were nice people. And when Steiner and I, my brother that's living now in Park, we had been to school up at 1910. We'd been to prepare to school, you see, taking up finishing up our seventh and eighth grade. We finished that in eight months there. That's the longest term we ever had. And we'd come home to visit grandma and grandpa. I guess that was during the Christmas vacation. It was in the winter. We got to Deary. Well this preacher ... had us come there. They treated us sociable, you know, give us meal. It was nice and friendly. Then my uncle come out, get us, he had to come with a team, you see, to get us into Park where the grandparents was. And of course we got in there. Then there was young couples over there dancing and that's something we already knew how to dance.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: We joined with the crowd, you know, and have a big time. See I was 22 then… steiner was 20.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But the thing is, to me, that's kind of interesting is that you didn't get married for a few years.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I was 25. 25 boy got married three years afterwards.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you waiting for the right girl?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, not necessarily. No, not necessarily. Hell, I had girls on the ridge, but I didn't like them. No, sir. No, I had plenty of them, but I just couldn't see it until I met the right one. Something just come over me. That was the one… is that funny… see, when she was in that choir, that's when I got that feeling. And she was, she used to play an organ herself. But she was up there with the choir singing. And she was dressed in white. And let's see, well I got a picture of, where's that young picture? I think I got a young one here. I'll just show you for a minute. Oh, there's one up there. See, that's when we first married. Oh, yeah. That's our wedding picture right there… see? You hear… there's two of them. You know that this was taken at Spokane. And that guy that took that, gave us this. We bought two dozen small ones. Similar size. This, my parents here. See, she was only 18 and he was 25. That's my own parents. Mother and dad. That's her wedding picture. That's why I took it up there. They're above us. It's a beautiful little picture. You know, my relatives, I mean all my friends and all the, see that I, well, that, Steiner's oldest son and his wife. God, that wife of his says, Helmer says, I'm going to give you pictures. Says, the way you arrange them. He says, I just think it's wonderful. Come here, I'll show you their children. The place, yeah, that's all right. You told me now, Harvey Smith got you on the job. Yeah, well, I got 50 cents an hour on that. And it was only eight hours. That's four dollars a day, see.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: And, but I only get, wait a minute. Yeah, I did get that on that. That's what lifted me through. I paid ten dollars a month that winter for that house I rented on Polk Street… it's still there… and they were rocking Lewis Street down there. It's the one I remember the planers. You see, the only place they had street, I mean, pavement was in Main Street. That was in 38. No, wait a minute, 32. 32, 34, long in there. You know, them poles that are marked, I mean painted yellow with shows of street signs. That's one that WPA works. Of course, that time I only got, that's when I owned WPA in town. That only got 40 dollars a month. And both my family, see, and live on. But out there at the rock crushers, that was, I seemed like that only lasted. Well, it was, we were still working in 34 because that winter it rained all winter long.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: I can remember that. And they had to use four horses on one wagon. And the wagon sunk down halfway on the spokes when they were distributing these rocks in the street. They couldn't pull around and pitch them off. They just drove and had these planks. They'd open up the planks, don't you see? And one load would drop right here. Another one would go ahead and drop another one there, see? But I wasn't driving no team. I was out there pounding these big niggerheads so they could get them through the rock crusher with a 16 pound maul, don't you see? And that was a big sledge, square points, and if you hit little cockeyed it would break the handle.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's what a niggerhead was, huh?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, it was big rocks. You had to bust them so they could get them fed into the crusher. This old K-Mire was a foreman, you know, and I cracked this handle one day. And your bigger man and I was. And he says, well, and he talked kind of course. He says, boy, God, that ain't going to look very good on your check next in check. And I said, by God, you don't take that out of my check. I just talked right up to him. And he laughed. He knew better. He just tried to kid me, you see. And we got a long swell after that. Somebody told me, I don't know, quite a few of them kind of kidded about him. They said that he was a little overbearing. Some little fella had knocked him on his hind or I don't know whether they had or not. That could have been a stally too, you know. I never saw anything like it. I didn't see it happen, but it could have been.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of living in Moscow here after living in the country all your life? What did you think of living in here?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Well, I had to get, that's when I moved off the, when I went broke farming in Park. I had them 40-4 head of cattle at the bank taking for a thousand dollars that I owed them. But I quit the ridge, Dad's place, because I got out of debt with my hog money. I cleared up $4 ,400 that time. And Dad begged me to stay. I'd stayed there seven years. But the first few years I was going in behind, behind. We didn't bring much. The first bunch of hogs, like I told you, only brought me six cents.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: $12 for a 200 pound hog? But the thing is then, when you was in here and working in Moscow, what happened so far? Did the work change after three, four?

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: Oh, no, no, boy. Summertime, this was long in the winter when it was hard places to get jobs. I'll tell you, I sold sacks for Fred Reems out here, $4 a day, on board, 12 hours. And I sold sacks for Johnson out here in the country. He's out here with this, no, he lived down there, but he had farm over here for this Joe country, that mountain country. And then I went and sold sacks one year for, in the harvest, the fellow at Lewis, Palouse City. There I got bigger money because I could sew and hang my own sack for $6 a day on board. I'll have to tell you how I got that job. I come there in this old bottle of tea that I bought from Dad on this sale. And the old jalopy, you know, and I sat down on the street, and here were about 100 men sitting on the main street looking for work. I sat down alongside of an old timer there, and he got friendly right away.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He says, don't look very good, doesn't he? Oh my God, sure don't. I said, I look like there's much employment around here. He says, I wanted to know if I had two bits to let him have. He hadn't had no meal for a couple of days. I guess he was kind of a bummer, I don't know. But he was kind of aged, he had a little gray hair and all, so I felt sorry for him. Yeah, I said, I got two bits, I'll give him two bits. Them days you could buy a loaf of bread and a couple of cans of sardine, you know, make quite a little lunch. Then he got awful friendly and he said, have you got a place to sleep? No, I've carried our blankets. Them days you had to carry your blankets and harvest. Nobody kept you, you had to go sleep in a straw tank. I said, no, I haven't found a place. Well, he says, I know where there's a straw tank three miles out.

speaker: Helmer Ringsage
words: He says, what's the matter with going out there tonight? I said, fine. He said, he'd bet. Well, I got a bright idea, or thought I did.
